experiments.title: Stripping the training wheels
experiments.question: Earlier experiments told the specialists exactly which cautious phrases to use. What do they say when nobody scripts them?
experiments.approach: We rewrote every prompt to remove scripted wording and named categories, then re-measured how much caution and qualification actually survives into the final answer.
experiments.result: Unscripted specialists still qualify their claims, at roughly half the scripted rate — and only a small fraction of it survives the editor's rewrite into the final answer.
experiments.learning: Careful language in earlier results was partly an artifact of us dictating it. Measurement moved to unscripted setups from here on.

experiments.title: Rechecking an early claim about answer style
experiments.question: An early result claimed the panel's answer format changed how much caution appeared. Does it survive a clean re-test?
experiments.approach: Re-ran the comparison with the cleaned-up prompts and honest uncertainty accounting.
experiments.result: The re-test was too uncertain to confirm or deny the original claim — its uncertainty range contained both the old claim and zero.
experiments.learning: The original claim was withdrawn as unsupported, and the question was marked open rather than answered. Being unable to re-establish a claim is not the same as disproving it.

experiments.title: Planting a wrong number
experiments.question: If one specialist's analysis contains a wrong figure, does the editor repeat it in the final answer?
experiments.approach: We planted an incorrect value in one specialist's analysis and watched whether the final answer repeated it — with and without a second specialist covering the same figure correctly.
experiments.result: With a clean second source available, the wrong number got through 0 times in 27. With no clean source, it was repeated or silently dropped.
experiments.learning: The editor protects against errors only when a correct alternative exists in front of it. Protection is coverage.

experiments.title: The panel vs. one model on right-answer questions
experiments.question: Does the full panel beat a single strong model on questions with checkable answers?
experiments.approach: Both setups answered a 60-question battery with known correct answers, scored automatically.
experiments.result: Statistically indistinguishable — but both scored 92–97%, so there was almost no room to see a difference. Only three questions separated them at all.
experiments.learning: A comparison at the ceiling can't answer the question. This flaw shaped the design of the final accuracy showdown two dozen experiments later.

experiments.title: Does the editor actually recompute anything?
experiments.question: When the editor produces a number, is it re-deriving it or copying it from a specialist?
experiments.approach: Set up cases where recomputing and copying give different answers, and checked which one the final answer contained.
experiments.result: It copies. The 'editor recomputes' story was disproven: the editor is a chooser among sources, not a calculator.
experiments.learning: The word 'recomputation' was banned from the project's claims. Everything built later treats the editor as a source selector.

experiments.title: Caution from nowhere
experiments.question: Does the editor add cautious qualifications that no specialist ever wrote?
experiments.approach: Fed the editor specialist analyses verified to contain zero qualifications, then counted qualifications in its output using a validated two-judge check.
experiments.result: A third of final answers contained invented qualifications — caution with no upstream source.
experiments.learning: Some hedging in final answers is the editor's own habit, not transmitted expertise. You can't read a final answer's caution as the specialists' caution.

experiments.title: A second editor, same story
experiments.question: Do the transmission findings depend on our particular editor model?
experiments.approach: Re-ran key measurements with a different model in the editor's chair.
experiments.result: The same qualitative pattern held: heavy loss of specialist caution in transmission.
experiments.learning: The transmission problem is a property of the synthesis step, not a quirk of one model.

experiments.title: Ordering a specialist to flag uncertainty
experiments.question: If a specialist is directly instructed to rate its own confidence, do the ratings mean anything?
experiments.approach: Instructed specialists to self-rate and checked the ratings against actual behavior — with a hard look at whether the measurement itself was sound.
experiments.result: The measurement collapsed: a background quirk depressed all rates and made the comparison unreadable. Recorded as unmeasurable rather than spun either way.
experiments.learning: This failure produced a permanent checklist rule: before trusting any comparison, verify the measurement can actually detect the thing at the rates involved.

experiments.title: The phrase or the behavior?
experiments.question: When an instruction 'works,' did the model change behavior — or just start using the instruction's words?
experiments.approach: Separated exact-phrase compliance from behavior change across scripted and unscripted setups.
experiments.result: Dictated phrasing went from 0-in-30 to 28-in-30 outputs; behavior beyond the phrase barely moved.
experiments.learning: The sharpest early statement of the program's signature finding: an instruction installs its own words, not the disposition behind them.

experiments.title: The synonym swap
experiments.question: If instructing 'label estimates with phrase X' truly changes behavior, swapping X for a synonym shouldn't matter. Does it?
experiments.approach: Two versions of the pipeline differed only in which synonym the instruction named, against a control with no instruction. Everything else byte-identical.
experiments.result: Each version produced its own named phrase about two-thirds of the time and the other version's phrase never. Behavior outside the named phrase: statistically unchanged.
experiments.learning: Instructions buy the phrase and nothing measurable beyond it. Every later design stopped relying on 'be careful' instructions entirely.

experiments.title: Is a 'medical AI' actually medical?
experiments.question: Do specialist fine-tuned models share a distinctive domain approach that generalists lack?
experiments.approach: Compared medical fine-tunes against their own base models on in-domain and out-of-domain questions, measuring distinctive framework vocabulary. One candidate was disqualified before testing for producing near-empty answers.
experiments.result: The signatures are per-model, not per-specialty: two medical fine-tunes of the same base disagreed with each other, and a third pointed the opposite way.
experiments.learning: A specialty label predicts nothing. Seats on the panel must be earned by measurement, never granted by category — the origin of the qualification gate.

experiments.title: The blind taste test
experiments.question: Do readers actually prefer the panel's merged answer over one strong model answering alone? And what does cautious wording cost?
experiments.approach: Anonymous side-by-side matchups judged by an AI judge with the reading order flipped both ways, so neither answer got the first-position advantage.
experiments.result: The merged answer won 82% of decisive matchups — a real, large win. But the versions carrying instructed cautious phrasing lost to their own plain twin (26–32% win rates).
experiments.learning: Merging genuinely reads better — and the same judges punish visible caution. Whatever safety language a pipeline adds in-line, preference pressure will strip.

experiments.title: A second opinion on the taste test
experiments.question: Does the preference result survive a completely different family of AI judge?
experiments.approach: Re-judged every matchup with a judge from an unrelated model family, chosen before anyone knew which way it would lean.
experiments.result: The panel's win replicated (79%). The penalty for cautious phrasing replicated on one wording and pointed the same way on the other.
experiments.learning: The headline preference results are not one judge's taste. Also discovered en route: a raw single-order judge is mostly measuring reading order — always flip and require agreement.

experiments.title: Sending the editor back with a question
experiments.question: If a disagreement between specialists gets a targeted follow-up answer, does the editor use it?
experiments.approach: Planted a disagreement whose resolution required one specific fact. Compared: no follow-up, a follow-up containing the fact, and a same-length follow-up that sounded responsive but contained nothing.
experiments.result: With the informative follow-up the editor adopted the right resolution 7 times in 7, versus a third of the time with none — and the contentless follow-up did worse than nothing.
experiments.learning: The follow-up loop works because of information, not ritual. And empty replies may actively mislead — the origin of the reply checks.

experiments.title: Can a specialist raise its own hand?
experiments.question: Will a specialist recognize a question outside its expertise and point to the right colleague?
experiments.approach: Gave specialists a roster and a way to defer, then posed questions inside and outside their domains.
experiments.result: When they did defer, they pointed to the right colleague 10 times in 11. But they recognized that they should defer only about 30% of the time — and sometimes deferred their own specialty away.
experiments.learning: The skill exists; the self-awareness to invoke it doesn't. Follow-ups must be triggered by work products a model already produces reliably, never by its self-assessment.

experiments.title: The transmission law, second writer
experiments.question: Is the loss of specialist caution during synthesis a stable, transferable pattern?
experiments.approach: Measured the supply-to-survival relationship on fresh cases with a second editor model, judged by the validated two-judge protocol.
experiments.result: The pattern replicated: only 11–33% of supplied qualification survives into final prose, across two editors and two case collections.
experiments.learning: Prose synthesis is a lossy channel for caution — a law, not an anecdote. If assumptions matter, they cannot travel through the editor.

experiments.title: Engineering the safety net
experiments.question: If protection comes from coverage, does deliberately assigning a key figure to two specialists actually prevent errors?
experiments.approach: One factor changed: a corrupted figure was either sole-sourced or also covered correctly by a second specialist.
experiments.result: Error adoption halved (90% down to 45%) and the correct value was actively adopted, not just diluted. Protection was all-or-nothing per question, though — some items fully protected, others not at all.
experiments.learning: Redundancy works and can be engineered. Why some questions resist protection stayed an open mystery through two follow-up hunts.

experiments.title: Shipping assumptions in their own section
experiments.question: If the specialists' assumptions are attached in a dedicated section instead of woven into prose, do they survive? Do judges punish the section?
experiments.approach: Byte-identical answers with and without a mechanically attached assumptions section, run through the blind taste test.
experiments.result: The section carried 100% of the assumptions, versus 17% surviving through prose. The preference effect was too tie-heavy to call — no evidence of a penalty, no proof of none.
experiments.learning: The separate track solves the transmission problem outright. Whether anyone uses what it carries became the next question.

experiments.title: How does the editor pick between conflicting numbers?
experiments.question: When two specialists state different values, what decides the winner — plausibility, or whose domain it is?
experiments.approach: Planted conflicting values with controlled plausibility and domain placement, then looked for a pattern.
experiments.result: Neither theory survived: both effects were too uncertain to call. A striking specialist-loyalty pattern appeared after the fact — flagged for a confirmation test rather than believed.
experiments.learning: Patterns found while explaining your own data need a fresh test before they count. The next experiment existed to provide one.

experiments.title: The loyalty theory meets fresh data
experiments.question: Does the editor's apparent loyalty map — which specialist 'owns' which figure — predict its choices on new questions?
experiments.approach: Elicited the editor's own stable ownership opinions first, froze them as predictions, then tested on fresh conflicts with placement counterbalanced.
experiments.result: Exactly a coin flip: 50%. The editor holds a confident, reproducible opinion about who owns what — and that opinion does not govern its behavior.
experiments.learning: The confirmation test did its job: it killed a plausible law before it calcified. Twice now, a model's stable self-report failed to predict its actions.

experiments.title: Does anyone read the assumptions section?
experiments.question: A caveat delivered only in the attached section — does it change a reader's actual decision?
experiments.approach: Planted decision-relevant caveats and asked a reader model for a one-word go/no-go, across four delivery setups including a decoy section carrying an irrelevant caveat. Some caveats blocked the obvious call, others enabled it, so pure caution couldn't fake the effect.
experiments.result: The relevant caveat flipped decisions 73% of the time; the decoy section moved them 4%. Delivering in the section worked as well as weaving into prose.
experiments.learning: The assumptions section is read and acted on — content-specific, at no loss versus prose. The separate track is engineering, not decoration.

experiments.title: Do specialists contaminate each other?
experiments.question: Our rule kept specialists from seeing each other's work, fearing they'd drift out of their lanes. Is the fear real?
experiments.approach: One factor changed: identical colleague analyses either shown or hidden, with lane drift measured by out-of-domain vocabulary.
experiments.result: Nothing. Drift moved by less than a hundredth against a test sensitive enough to catch a third of the everyday level. If anything, specialists who saw colleagues' coverage stayed slightly narrower.
experiments.learning: Our own design rationale was wrong, and we published that. The isolation rule survives only because sharing costs compute, not because sharing corrupts.

experiments.title: A live follow-up, first attempt
experiments.question: Can a real specialist — not a scripted stand-in — answer the editor's follow-up usefully?
experiments.approach: Buried each deciding fact inside the specialist's own earlier analysis, then ran the full loop live.
experiments.result: Stopped at the safety checks we'd set in advance: with the fact visibly in the pile, the editor rarely flagged the disagreement at all (about 1 in 5), so the loop had nothing to work with.
experiments.learning: Two real findings from a halted experiment: specialists resurface their own buried facts reliably when asked, and a briefed fact gets ignored unless the task actually calls for it.

experiments.title: A live follow-up, done right
experiments.question: Same question, corrected design: the specialist holds the deciding fact privately — knowledge it has but never wrote down.
experiments.approach: The editor's follow-up went to a live specialist holding the fact only in private notes; everything else ran exactly as the original loop experiment.
experiments.result: The specialist conveyed the fact 21 times in 21, and the editor adopted the right resolution 90% of the time versus 33% without the loop — nearly matching the scripted ideal.
experiments.learning: The full loop works end-to-end with no scripted parts. One dark spot: a few live replies decorated the true fact with invented citations — and the editor believed them.

experiments.title: Does the qualification gate actually predict anything?
experiments.question: We screen models before seating them. Does a screening verdict forecast real behavior in the pipeline?
experiments.approach: Screened ten local models on separate warm-up questions, locked the verdicts publicly, then seated every model on the real cases.
experiments.result: Perfect rank separation: both screen-failers broke down in the pipeline (33% and 94% defect rates); all eight passers ran essentially clean. One model that passed an old screen failed a fresh one — and then failed in the pipeline exactly as the fresh screen predicted.
experiments.learning: The gate forecasts, it doesn't just describe. And screening verdicts age: always re-test, never trust a stored pass.

experiments.title: How often do specialists make things up?
experiments.question: A specialist under pressure invented court cases. How often does that happen, and why?
experiments.approach: 120 live replies with and without the real fact in hand, every suspicious citation individually checked and classified.
experiments.result: Fabrication ran 10–15% of replies — but concentrated almost entirely on one trigger topic, with the same two invented court cases recurring across independent tries. Not one reply admitted to missing information.
experiments.learning: Invention is topic-triggered and eerily consistent, which makes a blocklist of known fakes a cheap, safe filter. The silence about gaps echoed every self-awareness failure before it.

experiments.title: Can the planner find what matters?
experiments.question: The safety net depends on a planner spotting the figures a decision turns on. Can it?
experiments.approach: The planner listed load-bearing figures for twelve cases, scored against independently authored answer keys, with a scrambled-case control to prove the test could fail.
experiments.result: It finds about 6 in 10 — and is best at exactly the right thing: figures that are missing (unmeasured rates, untracked inputs) get spotted 81% of the time, versus 53% for numbers printed on the page.
experiments.learning: The safety net is real but partial: protection extends to the figures the planner lists. Reading the specialists' work first didn't help it find more.

experiments.title: Planner-written assignments, first attempt
experiments.question: Does error protection survive when the planner writes the assignments itself?
experiments.approach: The planner divided the work live; test values were slipped to specialists via private notes.
experiments.result: Halted at the advance safety checks: specialists ignored private notes that had nothing to do with their assigned question — the notes only register when the task calls for them.
experiments.learning: A briefing channel isn't a megaphone; it rides on relevance. The corrected design gave the planner the target figure explicitly, as the real system would.

experiments.title: The safety net, fully live
experiments.question: With every link live — planner, specialists, editor — does the protection still work?
experiments.approach: The planner assigned a named figure to at least two specialists in every plan, values traveled by private notes, the editor synthesized. Compared against the scripted original.
experiments.result: The clean second source was used end-to-end: correct-value adoption rose 43 percentage points, nearly matching the scripted version's 50. Error suppression pointed the right way but couldn't be called — live prose already dilutes errors on its own.
experiments.learning: The half of protection that matters — the correct value actually winning — survives full automation. Forty of forty plans followed the coverage rule.

experiments.title: The accuracy showdown, round one
experiments.question: Built to escape the old ceiling problem: is the panel more accurate than one model on hard, checkable questions?
experiments.approach: 36 multi-step business calculations with machine-computed answers. A screening round required the single model to be beatable before any panel time was spent.
experiments.result: The single model scored 98%. Only 5 of 36 questions left any room to compete, so the showdown was called off before wasting the panel runs.
experiments.learning: Well-specified arithmetic is a solved problem for a strong model given room to think. 'Harder math' is a losing chase.

experiments.title: The accuracy showdown, round two — and the verdict
experiments.question: If not arithmetic, what about tangled rules — exceptions, precedence, waivers — with trivial math?
experiments.approach: 30 questions built as rule engines: the challenge is choosing and sequencing the right rules. Same screening round, with a pre-committed limit of two attempts total.
experiments.result: The single model scored 98.3% — higher still. Under the pre-committed rule, the question was closed: on well-specified questions there is no room for a panel to add accuracy, because one strong model already delivers it.
experiments.learning: The program's oldest open question resolved honestly: the panel's value was never accuracy. Its case rests entirely on three measured gains — readability, error protection, and resolved disagreements.

experiments.title: Old panel vs. new panel, head to head
experiments.question: After all the machinery — does the rebuilt panel's answer actually read better or worse than the original's?
experiments.approach: 54 fresh full runs of the rebuilt panel against archived answers from the original, in the blind taste test with two judge families.
experiments.result: A draw: most matchups tied, neither side won convincingly, and big effects were ruled out both ways. The assumptions section nudged answers slightly up, not down. On real questions, the follow-up loop fired 85% of the time — far above lab rates.
experiments.learning: The safety machinery ships free: same reader appeal, plus an audit trail, error protection, and a fabrication filter. That's the closing argument — buy the panel for trust, not brilliance.
